title: Rubio Orders Iran's Delegation Out of New York as Talks Stall
excerpt: U.S. officials say Iran's U.N. team had "overstayed their welcome" after indirect talks on the war and the Strait of Hormuz reached an impasse; Tehran insists the departure was pre-scheduled.
body:
• U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio ordered Iran's delegation, led by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, to leave New York on Monday after indirect talks aimed at ending the seven-month war reached a stalemate.
  • A U.S. official told Axios the delegation had "overstayed their welcome" after the UN General Assembly concluded; the team flew to Doha early Tuesday.
  • Iran's UN mission denied any expulsion, saying the departure followed a schedule communicated to the State Department on September 17 and accusing Washington of spreading "baseless and worthless" reports.
  • Qatari mediators spent days shuttling between the sides over Iran's nuclear program, the Strait of Hormuz, sanctions and a U.S. naval blockade — and continue to talk to both sides.

WASHINGTON — U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio ordered Iran's delegation to the United Nations General Assembly to leave New York immediately on Monday evening after indirect negotiations aimed at ending the seven-month war reached a stalemate, according to Axios, with the Associated Press later confirming the order with U.S. officials.

The U.S. mission to the U.N. notified Iran's U.N. mission that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his delegation were required to leave New York "immediately," two U.S. officials said. The Iranian delegation departed for Doha early Tuesday.

"Secretary Rubio kicked out the Iranian delegation who had overstayed their welcome. The UN General Assembly was over, so it was time for them to go," a U.S. official told Axios.

Context & Background

The Trump administration had granted tightly restricted visas for Iranian leaders to attend the annual U.N. meeting despite the ongoing hostilities. President Masoud Pezeshkian left after his speech, while Araghchi stayed for mediated contacts with Washington on the Strait of Hormuz, a wider ceasefire, and Iran's nuclear program.

Qatari mediators spent days shuttling between the sides in an effort to bridge differences over the nuclear program, the U.S. naval blockade, and the Strait of Hormuz. The White House had hoped for progress during Monday morning's session, but by the afternoon it was clear the negotiations were at an impasse.

President Donald Trump said Saturday that Iran had submitted a proposal during the talks — and that he rejected it. Tehran had offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and return to nuclear negotiations in exchange for sanctions relief and an end to the U.S. naval blockade; American negotiators turned those terms down.

"It is stuck. The Iranians are asking for things the U.S. can't accept and the U.S. thinks it is winning so there is no need for compromise."

— A source familiar with the negotiations, via Newsmax

Tehran disputes the American version. Iran's U.N. mission said the delegation left Monday evening "in accordance with the schedule" communicated to the State Department on September 17, accusing Washington of "propagating baseless and worthless news."

Impact & Analysis

The move is a highly unusual diplomatic rebuke, and it exposed how far apart the two sides remain even as Qatari mediators keep a compromise on the table. The conflict began on February 28; the administration initially predicted it would last roughly four to five weeks. More than seven months later, Trump is again predicting a quick end — paired with threats.

"Maybe I will blow 'em up," Trump told reporters Wednesday when asked about reaching an agreement with Tehran. "Maybe I blow 'em up. We have to make that decision. We will blow 'em up or make a deal. But the time is coming. It's gonna end very soon one way or the other."

"We will blow 'em up or make a deal. But the time is coming. It's gonna end very soon one way or the other."

— President Donald Trump, speaking to reporters

In an interview with Time published Thursday, Trump answered "possible" when asked whether he would ramp up bombing after the midterms — and "possible" again when asked whether he "might annihilate Iran." With the November 3 midterms approaching, rising energy costs tied to Hormuz disruptions have become an election issue; four Republican senators joined Democrats in backing a war powers measure, which failed 49-50.

Diaspora Angle

Before the war, roughly one-fifth of global crude oil and liquefied natural gas passed through the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint for much of India's oil imports — so continued disruption feeds directly into fuel prices in India and in the Gulf states hosting millions of Indian workers.

What's Next

Qatari mediators are continuing to talk to both sides about a compromise proposal, according to regional sources. Trump says the standoff will end "very soon one way or the other" — which leaves two opposite outcomes on the table: a deal that would ease the oil risk premium, or fresh strikes. What to watch: whether the mediators can reconvene the parties on new terms, and whether Trump's "after the midterms" timeline becomes a hard deadline.
image_caption: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi speaks at the United Nations in New York. Secretary of State Marco Rubio ordered Iran's delegation to leave the city as nuclear talks stalled.
nri_angle: The Hormuz standoff affects oil prices tied to India's imports, and the Qatari mediation runs through Doha, home to one of the region's largest Indian expatriate communities.
